title: Review: DNA replication; Genes, the genetic code and genomes
specRef: CC5(g), CC5(h); CC5(h); CC5(g), CC5(i), CC5(j), CC5(k) and others
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GE01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; GE01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; GE03#t2 term and clue written for the game; GE01a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: GE01a#N.4a, GE01b#N.9, GE03#N.5a, GE01a#N.6a, GE01b#N.10, GE03#N.3a, GE01a#N.2a, GE01b#N.7, GE01a#N.8. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Interphase
items.clue: Period before a cell divides, in which its DNA is copied.

items.label: Hybrid DNA
items.clue: Intermediate band: one ¹⁵N strand paired with one ¹⁴N strand.

items.label: Start codon
items.clue: AUG: sets where reading begins, and also specifies methionine.

items.label: DNA polymerase
items.clue: Enzyme that joins nucleotides to each other to build the new strand.

questions.stem: A drug inhibits helicase but has no effect on DNA polymerase. What will happen to DNA replication in a cell treated with the drug?

options.text: Replication continues normally, because DNA polymerase unwinds the double helix itself as it copies each strand.
New strands are made but fall off the template, because helicase forms the hydrogen bonds that hold new bases in place.
Cell division continues without replication, because the existing DNA is simply shared between the two daughter cells.
Replication cannot begin, because the hydrogen bonds between the strands are not broken, so no template strand is exposed.

questions.stem: In the Meselson–Stahl experiment, which result after one generation in ¹⁴N would have supported the conservative model?

options.text: One band, of intermediate density.
Two bands of equal amount, one heavy and one light.
One band, heavy.
Two bands of equal amount, one intermediate and one light.

questions.explanation: Conservative keeps the parent molecule whole (heavy) and makes a completely new one (light): two bands, equal amounts.

questions.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?

options.text: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.
Some amino acids are coded for by two bases and some by three bases.

questions.explanation: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids; for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.

questions.stem: During replication, a section of a template strand with the base sequence TACGGA is copied. Which statement describes the new strand built on this section?

options.text: Its sequence is TACGGA, an exact copy of the template strand it was assembled on.
Its sequence is AUGCCU, because uracil replaces thymine in each newly made strand.
Its sequence is ATGCCT, held to the template by covalent bonds made by DNA polymerase.
Its sequence is ATGCCT, the complement of the template, held to it by hydrogen bonds.

questions.explanation: A pairs with T and G with C, so the new strand reads ATGCCT and is held to the template by hydrogen bonds between paired bases.

questions.stem: The experiment is run in reverse. Bacteria are grown for many generations on light nitrogen (¹⁴N), then moved to a medium containing only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N). Replication is semi-conservative. What will the DNA show after two generations on ¹⁵N?

options.text: Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and light.
Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and heavy.
One band, between intermediate and heavy.
Two bands: one quarter light, three quarters heavy.

questions.explanation: Generation 1: every molecule is one light + one heavy strand (intermediate). Generation 2: 4 molecules, 2 hybrids holding the old light strands and 2 all-heavy.

questions.stem: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?

options.text: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.

questions.explanation: 4 × 4 = 16 is fewer than 20; 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 is more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

questions.stem: A cut in the skin heals as new skin cells are produced by cell division. Why must DNA replication take place before each of these divisions?

options.text: So that the existing DNA can be divided equally, half going to each of the new cells.
So that each new cell receives a complete copy of the DNA with an identical base sequence.
It does not need to take place, because replication is only required for reproduction.
So that the original DNA can stay intact in one cell and the other cell gets a new copy.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule in which both strands contain only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) is replicated three times in a medium that supplies only light nitrogen (¹⁴N), producing 8 DNA molecules. How many of the 8 DNA molecules contain any ¹⁵N?

options.text: 1 of 8
8 of 8
2 of 8
4 of 8

questions.explanation: In round 1 the two ¹⁵N strands separate and each pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand. They stay intact in every later round, so after round 3, 2 molecules contain ¹⁵N and 6 contain only ¹⁴N.

questions.stem: A short section of a DNA molecule has one strand reading GATTC, paired base by base with a second strand reading CTAAG. The molecule is replicated once. Which statement describes the two DNA molecules produced?

options.text: Each is GATTC paired with CTAAG; each has one strand of the original molecule and one new strand.
Each is GATTC paired with CTAAG; one has both original strands and the other has two new strands.
One is GATTC paired with GATTC and the other is CTAAG paired with CTAAG.
One gets the bases GAT paired with CTA, and the other gets TC paired with AG.

questions.explanation: Each original strand was a template for a new, complementary partner. Both molecules match the parent, and each keeps one original strand: semi-conservative.
